notes:
I could only finish a small part of this. The search tool hit its usage limit after one search and one page read, so these notes come from a single source: David Guzik's Enduring Word commentary on Psalm 14. That page also quotes several older teachers, and I've named them as Guzik quotes them. I didn't read their own pages.

That means two of your three sections are empty:
- **Differences between Protestant traditions (section 2):** I found nothing to report. Guzik quotes Spurgeon (Baptist) and Boice (Reformed), but that isn't the same as comparing traditions from their own teachers.
- **Other views (section 3):** I found nothing to report either. That covers modern scholarship, Catholic and Orthodox readings, and popular modern teaching.

Guzik works from the NKJV, so his wording is sometimes different from the BSB.

All points below are from: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-14/

---

**Title / overview**
- Guzik takes "the Chief Musician" (BSB: "choirmaster") as more than a human choir leader. He thinks it also points to God as the ultimate Musician.
- He sums up the psalm through G. Campbell Morgan: godliness is safe and ungodliness is dangerous.

**v. 1: "The fool says in his heart, 'There is no God'"**
- The Hebrew word for "fool" points to a moral failure, not a lack of intelligence. It means someone who rejects God, not someone too slow to understand Him.
- Kidner (as quoted) says the word is *nabal*, which suggests a stubborn, aggressive perversity. He links it to the man named Nabal in 1 Samuel 25:25.
- Boice (as quoted) points out that the Hebrew literally says "No God," meaning "no God for me." That is atheism in practice as well as in theory: the fool lives by his denial.
- "In his heart" matters. The fool wishes God away for moral reasons rather than intellectual ones. Guzik ties this to John 3:20, where those who do evil avoid the light. He also links it to Romans 1, where creation and conscience show that God is there.
- A person can believe in God in his mind but deny Him in how he lives. Guzik calls this a "practical atheist." He suggests David himself came close to this in 1 Samuel 27:1. Maclaren (as quoted) says that leaving God out of everyday life is what the psalmist mainly means.
- For witnessing, Guzik follows Spurgeon: speak to the doubter's heart, not only his head.
- Guzik lists reasons the God-denier is foolish and briefly sets out the classic arguments for God's existence.
- "They are corrupt... none who does good": Denying God leads to corrupt living. Guzik doesn't claim every atheist lives worse than every believer, but he sees a clear moral difference between those who take God seriously and those who don't.
- "None who does good" doesn't mean there is no human goodness at all. It means fallen people don't do good by instinct, and even their good deeds are mixed with evil.

**v. 2: "The LORD looks down from heaven..."**
- People may forget God, but God never stops watching them. Wanting God to leave us alone is unwise, because all life depends on Him (Acts 17:28; Matthew 5:45). It is also impossible, because He has a Creator's rights over what He made.
- Kidner (as quoted) hears an echo of God coming down to inspect Babel (Genesis 11:5) and of His survey of human wickedness before the Flood.
- God's search for anyone who "understands" or "seeks" Him is a moral and spiritual test, not an intellectual one.
- Guzik argues that left to themselves, people don't seek the true God. The world's religions don't prove otherwise, because when people start the search themselves, they end up with an idol of their own making. Spurgeon (as quoted) warns against empty religion that goes through the forms without ever meeting God.

**v. 3: "All have turned away... not even one"**
- Poole (as quoted) notes that "turned aside" can also mean "gone sour."
- Trapp (as quoted) notes that Hebrew uses related words for sin, a corpse and a stench.
- This verse widens the charge from the outspoken atheist to everyone, including religious people. Kidner (as quoted) says the atheist of verse 1 is just one example of humanity as a whole.
- Spurgeon (as quoted) makes one exception: the places where God's grace is at work. Guzik also links this verse to Romans 3.

**v. 4: "Will the workers of iniquity never learn?..."**
- God's people may look like the weak fools, but the evildoers are the ones who truly lack knowledge. Maclaren (as quoted) hears surprise in the question, as if even God wondered at people's love of evil.
- "Devour my people like bread": Poole (as quoted) explains that they do it as easily, eagerly and regularly as eating a meal, without remorse.
- "Refuse to call upon the LORD": Maclaren (as quoted) says atheism in practice is always prayerless.

**v. 5: "There they are, overwhelmed with dread..."**
- The wicked look confident, but underneath they are afraid. They know they are fighting God and can't win.
- Spurgeon (as quoted) says the Hebrew literally reads "they feared a fear." He describes it as a sudden, unexplained terror that even hardened people feel when conscience strikes.

**v. 6: "You sinners frustrate the plans of the oppressed, yet the LORD is their shelter"**
- David speaks directly to the evildoers. They may work against the poor, but God is a refuge for them that can't be broken into.
- Spurgeon (as quoted) lists four places the poor man gets his "counsel":
  - his own weakness, which drives him to God
  - what he sees of how the wicked end
  - the Bible
  - his experience of answered prayer
- Spurgeon also applied the verse to believers who are mocked at work. He urged them to stand firm and not be laughed out of their faith.

**v. 7: "Oh, that the salvation of Israel would come from Zion!..."**
- David knows God protects His people, but he can't see the victory yet, so he longs for it.
- "Restores His captive people": Guzik says this isn't about the Babylonian exile, which came long after David. "Captivity" here means any time God's people are oppressed. Maclaren (as quoted) uses Job 42:10 and Ezekiel 16:53 to read it as rescue from misfortune.
- David looks ahead to the rescue and calls God's people to rejoice.

---

The pages I planned to read next were Gill, Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary (biblehub/studylight), Precept Austin, the NET Bible notes, Augustine on Psalm 14 (newadvent.org), and Reformed and Wesleyan readings of verses 1–3 alongside Romans 3. If you run this again, those should fill the gaps, especially section 2, where verses 1–3 are the most likely place for real differences between traditions.
